ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the local ethics committee (approval number #413).

In an online study, N = 263 unselected participants completed a novel task in which each trial paired an expectancy sentence and rating with a subsequent interpretation sentence and rating, jointly assessing both processes.
After the task, participants completed self-report measures of IU, anxiety sensitivity, depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms, and general willingness to take risks.
A total of N = 314 participants took part in the study online, via Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/).

All participants completed the study within the expected time window (median: 59 minutes for the task, 6 minutes for the questionnaires).

Participants were asked to rate their agreement level with each item using a five-point Likert scale (0 = very little,4 = very much, e.g., 'When I cannot keep my mind on a task, I worry that I might be going crazy').
First, participants were asked to sign the consent form.
After the experimental task, participants were automatically redirected to the questionnaires.
Once done, participants were automatically redirected to Prolific with a dedicated submission code.

To this aim, an unselected sample of N = 263 participants completed a novel validated task online, in which participants read emotional and neutral scenarios reflecting sequentially linked expectancy and interpretation processes.
The current study adopted the assumption that, in an unselected sample, participants are likely rate positive outcomes are more expected than negative outcomes.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A total of N = 314 participants took part in the study online, via Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/). Sample size was determined using Schoemann's Shiny App for Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects (Schoemann et al., 2017). The analysis was conducted for a one-mediator model with a target power of 0.80. Standardized coefficients for the three paths were set to detect a small-to-medium effect size of 0.20, and the standard deviations of the three variables were set to 1. The results indicated that a minimum of N = 260 participants would be needed to detect the indirect effect (a*b). The study was approved by the local ethics committee (approval number #413). Data were collected between November 2025 and January 2026.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Expectancy and Interpretation Biases in Intolerance of Uncertainty
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: The current study will employ a scenario rating task to measure positive and negative expectancy and interpretation biases. Mediation analyses will be conducted separately on each emotional valence (positive and negative). Hypotheses are as following: 1. A higher level of expectancy bias is positively associated with higher interpretation bias (path a). 2. Interpretation bias has a direct effect on trait IU when controlling for expectancy bias (path b). 3. Expectancy bias has a direct effect on trait IU when controlling for interpretation bias (path c'). Taken together, interpretation bias is expected to partially mediate the relationship between expectancy bias and trait IU, meaning that both a direct effect of expectancy bias and an indirect effect through interpretation bias are expected to be found (a*b). Correlational analyses will also be conducted to examine the relationship between both biases and individual traits and within individual traits (intolerance of uncertainty, depression, anxiety and stress, anxiety sensitivity, and risk aversion). Correlations are expected to differ between the valences.
table.design_dependent_variables: Subjective ratings: During the scenario rating task, neutral and emotional scenarios will be presented. Each scenario is made out of two sentences: an expectancy sentence and an interpretation sentence. Each ambiguous incomplete sentence stem will be followed by a target word which would disambiguate it. A word can be congruent (positive in the emotional condition, expected in the neutral condition) or incongruent (negative in the emotional condition, unexpected in the neutral condition). After each sentence, a rating scale of 1-6 will appear, with the following question: "How much did you expect this outcome before you saw it?" The ratings of both the negatively and positively valenced expectancy and interpretation sentences will reflect the magnitude if the corresponding bias (i.e., positive/negative expectancy/interpretation). Importantly, while the two sentences in each scenario share a theme, their outcomes are unrelated. The following individual traits will be measures via questionnaires: trait intolerance of uncertainty (IUS), anxiety, depression and stress symptoms (DASS-21), anxiety sensitivity (ASI 3), global risk aversion.
table.study_design_overview: Participants will take part in a scenario rating task. All conditions are within-subject conditions, with the following variables: • Valence of scenario: emotional, neutral • Expectancy sentence outcome: congruent (positive for emotional, expected for neutral) / incongruent (negative for emotional, unexpected for neutral) • Interpretation sentence outcome: congruent (positive for emotional, expected for neutral) / incongruent (negative for emotional, unexpected for neutral)
table.statistical_tests: Manipulation check: a paired samples t-test will be used to make sure that neutral sentences with expected outcomes were indeed rated as more expected than neutral sentences with unexpected outcomes. Mediation analysis: The relationship between expectancy bias, interpretation bias, and trait IU will be analyzed using mediation analysis. Each valence (positive and negative) will be analyzed separately. Correlations: correlational analyses will be conducted between the 4 types of cognitive biases (i.e., positive/negative expectancy/interpretation) and questionnaire data.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
(1) Comprehension questions will be presented after 50% of the trials during the scenario rating task. (2) We will examine the ratings of neutral expected and unexpected outcomes. Participants will be excluded from analysis if they have a standard score of ±3 SD or higher for either criterion: comprehension question response accuracy and neutral ratings (i.e., if they rate expected outcomes as unexpected or vice versa). (3) Questionnaires will include attention checks that use the same response scale as the questionnaire. Each questionnaire will include one attention check. Participants will be excluded if they answer 2 or more out the 3 questions incorrectly. Of note, all sentences will be pre-validated in a pilot study.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
Sample size was determined using Schoemann's Shiny app for Monte Carlo Power Analysis for Indirect Effects. The analysis was conducted for a one-mediator model with a target power of 0.80. Standardized coefficients for the three paths were set to detect a small-to-medium effect size of 0.20, and the standard deviations of the three variables were set to 1. The results indicated that a minimum of 260 participants would be needed to detect the indirect effect (a*b). To account for potential technical issues and exclusions, a total of N = 300 unselected participants will be included in the study.

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
Moderated mediation: To examine whether the relationship between expectancy and interpretation is moderated by the valence of the sentence (positive/negative), we will conduct a moderated mediation analysis on path a (expectancy bias -> interpretation bias). Reaction time: correlational analyses will be conducted between reaction times of entering a rating and the actual rating score to examine whether there is an associative match (e.g., the more expected an outcome is, the faster the reaction time to complete the rating).

text.text: Expectancy and interpretation biases are widely considered transdiagnostic markers of psychopathology, yet the nature of their relationship remains understudied.
If these processes are causally related, modifying one may influence the other and reduce associated symptoms.
Intolerance of uncertainty (IU) is a transdiagnostic trait linked to biased interpretations and their modification.
The present study tested a mediation model in which interpretations were hypothesized to mediate the relationship between expectancies and IU.
According to this account, expectancy-related ratings were expected to predict interpretation-related ratings, which in turn were expected to predict trait IU.

In an online study, N = 263 unselected participants completed a novel task in which each trial paired an expectancy sentence and rating with a subsequent interpretation sentence and rating, jointly assessing both processes.
Sentence valence (neutral/emotional) and expectancy-interpretation outcome pairings (e.g., positive-positive, positive-negative) varied randomly across trials.

Results showed that more negative expectancy and interpretation ratings were associated with higher levels of trait IU, anxiety, and depression, whereas more positive ratings were associated with lower levels of each.
In a cross-sectional mediation model, expectancies showed significant direct paths to both interpretations and IU, but interpretations did not mediate the expectancy-IU relationship.
These findings point to a central transdiagnostic role for expectancies relative to interpretations.

Interventions may therefore benefit from prioritizing expectancy biases; nonetheless, the observation that expectancy and interpretation biases were associated with symptom measures in opposing and complementary directions indicates that joint assessment of both cognitive processes remains more informative than assessing either alone.
Everyday life is inherently filled with uncertainties and ambiguous situations, and individuals tend to differ in how much they can tolerate such ambiguity.
This trait refers to individual levels of intolerance of uncertainty (IU; Einstein, 2014).

text.text: Some individuals often expect negative outcomes of future situations (e.g., "If I go to the party alone, then I will probably look awkward"; Aue, 2021).
text.formatted: Some individuals often expect negative outcomes of future situations (e.g., "If I go to the party alone, then I will probably look awkward"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aue, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Such a negative a-priori expectancy bias may then affect the way in which subsequent ambiguous experiences are interpreted (e.g., "The person I met at the party ended our conversation because I looked awkward").
The tendency to interpret ambiguous information consistently in a negative manner is termed "negative interpretation bias" (Hirsch et al., 2016; Woud, 2022).
text.formatted: The tendency to interpret ambiguous information consistently in a negative manner is termed "negative interpretation bias" <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hirsch et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Woud, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This negative interpretation bias may, in turn, contribute to elevated levels of trait IU.
While expectancies are future-oriented, interpretations typically resolve ambiguity within the present.
IU, in contrast, is an individual predisposition which may interact with various cognitive processes across different stages of information processing.

The three concepts, expectancy bias, interpretation bias, and trait IU, characterize many mental and emotional disorders, and are thus recognized to be transdiagnostic risk factors (Einstein, 2014; Rief et al., 2015; Würtz et al., 2026).

text.text: This empirical knowledge, in turn, informs the development of interventions in the context of cognitive behavioral therapy.

For instance, a fundamental treatment element across anxiety disorders involves the modification of biased expectancies and interpretations, with the aim of producing downstream reductions in emotional symptoms (Woud & Hofmann, 2023).

text.text: Behaviorally, it has been suggested that both biased expectancies and interpretations lead to avoidance of potentially threatening situations.
This avoidance can create a vicious cycle, in which anxious individuals are unable to make correcting experiences, which, in turn, may reinforce both biases (Aue, 2021; Woud, 2022).
text.formatted: This avoidance can create a vicious cycle, in which anxious individuals are unable to make correcting experiences, which, in turn, may reinforce both biases <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aue, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Woud, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Although expectancy and interpretation biases have often been studied separately, some researchers have advocated studying the interplay between cognitive biases, noting that it is more informative and impactful to study both their unique and shared effects, compared to studying each bias in isolation (e.g., Abado et al., 2020; Hirsch et al., 2006).

text.text: For instance, it has been found that comorbid expectancy and interpretation biases predict high levels of social anxiety and alcohol use disorder (Chow et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For instance, it has been found that comorbid expectancy and interpretation biases predict high levels of social anxiety and alcohol use disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chow et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, it is important to examine the unique characteristics and temporal orientation of each bias.

By definition, expectancies concern hypothetical future outcomes, including the likelihood that specific valenced events and/or the severity of the consequences of such events (Aue, 2021; Ji et al., 2026; Ji & MacLeod, 2023).
text.formatted: By definition, expectancies concern hypothetical future outcomes, including the likelihood that specific valenced events and/or the severity of the consequences of such events <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aue, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Ji et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Ji & MacLeod, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, interpretation concerns attributing meaning to current ambiguous events (Grenier et al., 2005; Hirsch et al., 2016; Woud, 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, interpretation concerns attributing meaning to current ambiguous events <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Grenier et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hirsch et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Woud, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While previous findings have largely been derived from correlational studies, cognitive bias modification (CBM) paradigms allow for the testing of causal relationships by experimentally manipulating cognitive biases through systematic training (MacLeod & Mathews, 2012).
text.formatted: While previous findings have largely been derived from correlational studies, cognitive bias modification (CBM) paradigms allow for the testing of causal relationships by experimentally manipulating cognitive biases through systematic training <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(MacLeod & Mathews, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Although CBM typically targets a single bias, some studies assess transfer across biases.
Expectancy training can generalize to interpretations, with changes in expectancies accompanied by corresponding changes in interpretations (Frommelt et al., 2023; Krans et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Expectancy training can generalize to interpretations, with changes in expectancies accompanied by corresponding changes in interpretations <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Frommelt et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Krans et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For example, Krans et al. (2019) found that positive expectancy training, in which future-tense scenarios were consistently resolved positively, led to more positive interpretations on a subsequent task than did negative expectancy training.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Krans et al. (2019)</ref> found that positive expectancy training, in which future-tense scenarios were consistently resolved positively, led to more positive interpretations on a subsequent task than did negative expectancy training.

text.text: Thus, biased expectancies may shape subsequent interpretations, potentially creating a compounding cycle of avoidance and negative processing.
As trait IU involves distress in response to the inherent uncertainties and ambiguities of everyday life (Carleton, 2016), previous studies have linked IU with negative interpretation bias.
text.formatted: As trait IU involves distress in response to the inherent uncertainties and ambiguities of everyday life <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carleton, 2016)</ref>, previous studies have linked IU with negative interpretation bias.

text.text: While general interpretation bias paradigms typically target threat-related content (e.g., social or physical danger), IU-focused interpretation bias paradigms target the interpretation of uncertainty itself.
Their stimuli are built around uncertainty-laden cues, such as the words "Future," "Uncertainty," and "Doubt."

Using such a paradigm, higher IU has been found to be associated with greater negative interpretation bias, and IU-specific interpretation bias was further associated with social anxiety, general anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms (Oglesby et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Using such a paradigm, higher IU has been found to be associated with greater negative interpretation bias, and IU-specific interpretation bias was further associated with social anxiety, general anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Oglesby et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This reinforces the notion that both IU and interpretation bias correlate with symptoms of psychopathology, with potential transdiagnostic roles.

Randomized controlled trials show that IU-focused CBM targeting negative interpretation bias can reduce IU (Oglesby et al., 2017) and symptoms of worry and depression (Dugas et al., 2022) and anxiety (Li et al., 2021).

text.text: Taken together, these findings suggest the possibility of a directional sequence in which expectancy impacts interpretation, and interpretation impacts IU and transdiagnostic symptoms.

Of note, although most studies have focused on negatively biased cognitions, positively biased cognitions have also been investigated and are often considered adaptive (Aue & Okon-Singer, 2020) and potentially protective against depressive symptoms (Everaert et al., 2018).

text.text: Consistent with this perspective, both positive and negative interpretation biases could be targeted in treatment.

For instance, recent CBM studies targeting more positive interpretations found that, in CBM groups, positive interpretations increased and negative interpretations decreased after training (Abado et al., 2026; Ji et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For instance, recent CBM studies targeting more positive interpretations found that, in CBM groups, positive interpretations increased and negative interpretations decreased after training <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abado et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Ji et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, assessing and targeting both valences of these biases may have increased therapeutic value.
To summarize, studies highlight the transdiagnostic roles of expectancy bias, interpretation bias, and trait IU, yet most work has examined these factors separately.

Expectancy and interpretation biases appear to complement one another while also operating independently, and although expectancy bias has been linked to interpretation bias (Frommelt et al., 2023; Krans et al., 2019) and negative interpretation bias to IU (Oglesby et al., 2017; Tyson et al., 2025), no study has integrated all three in one design to clarify their unique and joint relationships.

text.text: It therefore remains unknown whether negative expectancy bias is associated with IU and whether interpretation bias mediates the link between expectancy bias and IU.
Clarifying these interrelations will help refine transdiagnostic models of cognitive vulnerability and will inform interventions that target expectancies, interpretations, or their link to reduce IU.
The current study examined the unique and shared contributions of expectancy and interpretation biases to trait IU, systematically manipulating the valence of each.
Previous work has often relied on separate measures for each process (e.g., Chan et al., 2020; Krans et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Previous work has often relied on separate measures for each process (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Chan et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Krans et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We therefore used a novel, pre-validated paradigm that assesses expectations about an upcoming outcome and the interpretation of ambiguity within the same event.
This allows a more direct and internally coherent test of positive and negative biases in both processes.
After the task, participants completed self-report measures of IU, anxiety sensitivity, depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms, and general willingness to take risks.
The latter was included as an exploratory measure because risk-taking willingness is associated with optimism (i.e., general positive expectancies; Dohmen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: The latter was included as an exploratory measure because risk-taking willingness is associated with optimism (i.e., general positive expectancies; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dohmen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It was hypothesized that the valence of expectancies directly affects the valence of subsequent interpretations.
For instance, a negative expectancy about the outcome of an upcoming event can bias how ambiguous aspects of the situation are interpreted as the event unfolds.
It is also hypothesized that both biases contribute to levels of trait IU, directly and indirectly.
Specifically, it was hypothesized that expectancies will be directly associated with trait IU and indirectly associated with trait IU via interpretations.

These hypotheses were expected to apply to both negative and positive biases in complementary directions: negative biases are expected to be associated with higher IU levels, whereas positive biases were expected to be associated with lower IU levels.

As secondary analyses, moderated mediation models tested whether associations among expectancy-related processing, interpretation-related processing, and trait IU differed for positive versus negative outcomes.

Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (UI-18; Freeston et al., 1994; German translation by Gerlach et al., 2008).

text.text: The UI-18 measures the degree to which individuals find uncertainty distressing and difficult to tolerate.

The German version of the IU scale comprises 18 items, which can be divided into three factors: limited ability to act due to intolerance of uncertainty (IU), burden caused by IU, vigilance when experiencing IU (e.g., 'I should be able to organize everything in advance').
Participants rate each item on a five-point Likert scale (1 = not at all characteristic for me,5 = entirely characteristic for me).

text.text: The DASS-21 is a questionnaire that measures symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress within the last week using a four-point Likert scale (0 = did not apply to me at all,3 = applied to me very much or most of the time, e.g., 'I couldn't seem to experience any positive feeling at all').
The DASS-21 comprises three subscales with seven items each.

text.text: The ASI-3 measures anxiety sensitivity and includes three subscales: physical concerns, cognitive concerns and social concerns, each including six items.

The Expectancy-Interpretation Rating Task assesses expectations about a potential future scenario, as well as interpretations of an ambiguous event occurring within that scenario (see Abado et al., 2026, for a similar task).

text.text: Participants read emotional and neutral scenarios.

Emotional scenarios described everyday, potentially anxiety-and worry-evoking situations (e.g., work, study, social performance and perception, health, and finance), whereas neutral scenarios described neutral situations, such as preparing food or doing housework.
Each scenario comprised two sequential sentences: an expectancy sentence and an interpretation sentence, designed to assess expectancies and interpretations, respectively.

Expectancy sentences were future-oriented and followed a fixed structure, while iinterpretation sentences were present-oriented and described an ambiguous event with an attributed cause (see Table 1 for examples).
text.formatted: Expectancy sentences were future-oriented and followed a fixed structure, while iinterpretation sentences were present-oriented and described an ambiguous event with an attributed cause (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for examples).

text.text: Each sentence initially appeared incomplete, followed by a short pause and then a final word that resolved the uncertainty or ambiguity (the outcome word).
After each sentence, participants rated on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = not at all,6 = very much) the extent to which they expected the outcome word before seeing it.
Each sentence had two versions that differed in outcome (see Table 1 for examples).
text.formatted: Each sentence had two versions that differed in outcome (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> for examples).

text.text: In an unselected sample, positive outcomes of emotional sentences were assumed to be more expected than negative ones.

Accordingly, "congruent" refers to emotional sentences with positive outcomes and neutral sentences with plausible outcomes, whereas "incongruent" refers to emotional sentences with negative outcomes and neutral sentences with implausible outcomes.
For neutral sentences, congruency was manipulated according to the objective logical plausibility of the outcome.
Each scenario (a pair of expectancy and interpretation sentences) therefore had four versions, randomly assigned to each participant while keeping the number of trials constant across conditions.

Scenarios were written so that expectancy and interpretation outcomes were logically independent: even if the expectancy sentence ended negatively, the interpretation sentence could equally plausibly resolve negatively or positively.
Thus, although the two sentences shared a theme, the valences of their outcomes were unrelated.
Neutral scenarios (29% of trials) served only as manipulation checks and were not of theoretical interest.
All sentences were validated in a separate study (N = 148), in which participants read each sentence with all possible outcomes and rated the outcomes.
For emotional sentences, participants rated the positivity and negativity of each ending.
For neutral sentences, they rated the expectedness of each ending.
Sentences with overlapping ratings (e.g., one outcome rated as equally expected and unexpected) or reversed patterns (e.g., a plausible outcome rated as unexpected) were excluded.
Results of this validation study will be published separately (Abado et al., in preparation).

text.text: The manipulation check tested whether neutral sentences with plausible outcomes were rated differently from those with implausible outcomes.

To this end, an LMM predicted responses from valence (emotional vs. neutral), bias (expectancy vs. interpretation), congruence (congruent vs. incongruent), and their interactions, with random intercepts for each participant.

Interaction terms were evaluated via model comparison, and the congruent vs. incongruent contrast for neutral sentences was extracted from the model as the primary outcome, with within-subject effect sizes (Hedges' g with 95% CIs).
All remaining main effects and interactions are reported in the Supplementary Materials for completeness.
Mediation Analysis.
Mediation analysis tested whether the association between expectancies and IU was mediated by interpretations.
Analyses were run only for emotional conditions, separately for each valence (positive and negative).
Predictor (expectancies) and mediator (interpretations) were measured at trial level, due to the experiment's design of matched expectancy and interpretation sentences in each trial.
The outcome (IU score) was participant level.
For path a (expectancies → interpretations), trial-level data was used with a LMM including random intercepts for participants.

For paths b and c′ (interpretations → IU and expectancies → IU, controlling for interpretations), participant-level data was used by averaging expectancy and interpretation ratings per participant, and estimated these paths with standard linear regression.
Mediation was tested using nonparametric bootstrap (5,000 simulations) to obtain confidence intervals for indirect, direct, and total effects.
As secondary analyses, moderated mediation models tested whether the expectancyinterpretation-IU pathways differed across positive versus negative outcomes.
These models included expectancy × interpretation interactions in path a and examined indirect effects separately for each valence condition.

text.text: Risk-taking willingness negatively correlated with the three questionnaires (rs = -.16 to -.35, ps ≤ .011).
The aim of the current study was to examine the relationships among expectancies, interpretations, and trait intolerance of uncertainty (IU).

We hypothesized that the valence of expectancies would affect the valence of subsequent interpretations, that both processes would be associated with IU, and that interpretation bias would account for part of the association between expectancy bias and IU in a mediation model.

To this aim, an unselected sample of N = 263 participants completed a novel validated task online, in which participants read emotional and neutral scenarios reflecting sequentially linked expectancy and interpretation processes.
Each scenario consisted of two thematically and temporally linked sentences -an expectancy sentence followed by an interpretation sentence -whose outcomes were logically unrelated.

Emotional or neutral sentences could end with either a congruent outcome (plausible for neutral scenarios, positive for emotional scenarios) or an incongruent outcome (implausible for neutral scenarios, negative for emotional scenarios).
One important finding served as a manipulation check.

Specifically, as intended, plausible and implausible neutral outcomes differed significantly, with a very large effect size: participants rated plausible outcomes as highly expected and implausible outcomes as highly unexpected.
For emotional sentences, participants rated positive outcomes as more expected than negative ones.
In this unselected sample, this pattern is consistent with the positivity bias previously reported in healthy individuals (Sharot, 2011).
text.formatted: In this unselected sample, this pattern is consistent with the positivity bias previously reported in healthy individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Sharot, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: A different pattern emerged in a sample with high social anxiety using a similar paradigm that assessed only interpretations: ratings differed between outcomes for neutral but not emotional sentences (Abado et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A different pattern emerged in a sample with high social anxiety using a similar paradigm that assessed only interpretations: ratings differed between outcomes for neutral but not emotional sentences <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abado et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The discrepancy likely reflects sample composition: individuals with high social anxiety may show attenuated positivity and a more negative interpretation profile.

In addition, the present paradigm required participants to process and rate both expectancies and interpretations within each scenario, which may have encouraged more elaborated scenario processing and, in this unselected sample, more positive interpretation ratings.
Complementary exploratory analyses (to be found in the Supplementary Materials) revealed two notable findings.

First, collapsed across valence and congruency conditions, contrasts indicated that expectancies and interpretations are qualitatively distinct, as ratings for expectancy and interpretation sentences differed.
The same is also true for contrasts within valences (e.g., emotional expectancy vs. emotional interpretation).
This suggests that the two processes may represent distinct cognitive mechanisms rather than simple continuations or resolutions of one another, although a strong association between them exists.
Second, clear differences emerged between neutral and emotional sentences.
Ratings for neutral sentences followed a relatively uniform pattern, whereas emotional sentences showed greater variability, likely reflecting individual differences.

This finding emphasizes the importance of using non-self-referential neutral stimuli as a reliable baseline in emotional tasks, which often instead use emotional sentences with benign endings (e.g., Feng et al., 2020) or self-referential neutral sentences, both of which may still evoke emotion (e.g., Moser et al., 2012).

text.text: The primary mediation analysis revealed that a significant path between expectancies and interpretations.
This association occurred only within the same valence: positive expectancies predicted positive interpretations, and negative expectancies predicted negative interpretations.
In line with our hypothesis, this finding suggests that the level of emotionally valenced expectations (positive vs. negative) is reflected in similarly valenced subsequent interpretations.

Second, as hypothesized, a direct link emerged between expectancies and IU for both valences: stronger negative expectancies were associated with higher IU, whereas stronger positive expectancies were associated with lower IU.
Finally, contrary to our hypothesis, interpretations did not mediate the relationship between expectancies and IU, and no direct association was found between interpretations and IU.
Thus, expectancies were independently associated with interpretations and IU in positive and negative scenarios.

Interestingly, correlations emerged within biases and between biases and with symptom measures: within biases, the higher the levels of positive expectancies, the higher the levels of positive interpretations and the lower the levels of negative expectancies.
Negative expectancies also highly correlated with negative interpretations.
Negative interpretations, on the other hand, did not correlate with positive interpretations, suggesting some dissociation between the two valences.

Significant correlations also emerged between cognitive biases and symptom measures, as positive and negative expectancies significantly correlated with all questionnaires, in opposing and complementing directions, where more negative expectancies were associated with higher levels of psychopathology, including trait IU, depression, stress and anxiety, and anxiety sensitivity.
Additionally, negative expectancies were associated with lower willingness to take risks.
While a similar pattern emerged for positive and negative interpretations, correlations between both interpretation valences and willingness to take risks were nonsignificant.
Lastly, all questionnaires correlated with each other.
Together, these correlations highlight the transdiagnostic nature of expectancies and interpretations, with expectancies showing somewhat stronger transdiagnostic associations.
These findings also highlight the transdiagnostic role of IU, as it is associated with general psychopathology symptoms as well as with differentially valenced cognitive processes (Einstein, 2014).
text.formatted: These findings also highlight the transdiagnostic role of IU, as it is associated with general psychopathology symptoms as well as with differentially valenced cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Einstein, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The results suggest a dissociation between the two processes: although interpretation and expectancy were strongly correlated within valence, interpretation was no longer associated with IU once expectancy was statistically controlled.
Interpretation thus explained no unique variance in IU beyond expectancy, suggesting that IU is more closely related to how expectations are formed than to interpretation bias per se.

By measuring both biases within the same task and modeling them jointly, the study shows that expectancy and interpretation, although closely related, differ in their relation to IU, a distinction that would be obscured if each bias were examined in isolation.
The differential associations of IU with expectancies and with interpretations align with prior work distinguishing intolerance of uncertainty from intolerance of ambiguity.

Although both constructs are related to worry and anxiety, the former is future-oriented, referring to potential negative future events, whereas the latter is present-oriented, referring to the negative interpretation of current events (for a review, see Grenier et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Although both constructs are related to worry and anxiety, the former is future-oriented, referring to potential negative future events, whereas the latter is present-oriented, referring to the negative interpretation of current events (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Grenier et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: A later review, however, considered this dissociation tentative and called for further evidence linking future-oriented expectancies with IU (Birrell et al., 2011).
text.formatted: A later review, however, considered this dissociation tentative and called for further evidence linking future-oriented expectancies with IU <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Birrell et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The current findings provide such evidence, supporting the notion that IU is more closely associated with futureoriented thinking than with present-oriented interpretation of ambiguity.
The current results differ somewhat from previous studies which causally linked negative interpretation bias with IU (Li et al., 2021; Oglesby et al., 2017).

text.text: Several factors may explain this discrepancy.

For instance, Oglesby et al. (2017) selected participants with elevated interpretation bias and used a multi-session training manipulation, whereas the current sample was unselected and cross-sectional.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Oglesby et al. (2017)</ref> selected participants with elevated interpretation bias and used a multi-session training manipulation, whereas the current sample was unselected and cross-sectional.

text.text: More speculatively, reductions in negative interpretation may have been accompanied by collateral reductions in negative expectancy, which the training paradigm neither targeted nor measured.

This is consistent with our findings that, although qualitatively distinct, expectancy and interpretation biases were highly correlated, and that expectancy, not interpretation, showed the more robust unique association with IU.
If interpretation training transfers to expectancy, an incidental reduction in expectancy bias could account for the reduction in IU observed in the trial.
Future studies could test this by assessing changes in both biases before and after IUfocused CBM training.

The present results thus point to expectancy as a candidate mechanism underlying the effects of interpretation-focused training on IU, and highlight the value of measuring both biases in future intervention studies to determine which change drives the reduction in IU.

The link between the biases and trait IU mirrors findings from a recent previous study, which examined the mediating role of expectancy bias in the link between attention bias and trait anxiety (Ventris et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The link between the biases and trait IU mirrors findings from a recent previous study, which examined the mediating role of expectancy bias in the link between attention bias and trait anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ventris et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In that study, both attention bias and expectancy biases were correlated with trait anxiety, yet the association between attention bias and trait anxiety was fully mediated by expectancy bias.
This parallels the present findings in that expectancy bias retained an independent link to the outcome (IU), while interpretation bias did not.
Of note, expectancy bias occupied a different structural role across the two models: a proximal mediator in (Ventris et al., 2026), and a distal predictor in the present study.
text.formatted: Of note, expectancy bias occupied a different structural role across the two models: a proximal mediator in <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ventris et al., 2026)</ref>, and a distal predictor in the present study.

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that expectancy bias may play a key role in downstream pathways of biased information processing, regardless of its position (predictor vs. mediator; see also Basanovic et al., 2024, and Ji & MacLeod, 2023, for evidence of the mediating role of expectancies in the relationship between psychopathology symptoms and subsequent behavioral choices and negative thoughts).

text.text: The convergence across different biases and outcome measures strengthens the view that expectancies are a robust pathway linking biased information processing to emotional vulnerability.
In line with previous research, the current study showed a link between positive expectancies and willingness to take risks (Dohmen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In line with previous research, the current study showed a link between positive expectancies and willingness to take risks <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Dohmen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, expectancies and interpretations showed a dissociation: willingness to take risks was positively associated with positive expectancies and negatively associated with negative expectancies.

Despite this complementary pattern of associations, willingness to take risks was not associated with interpretations of ambiguous stimuli, suggesting that it is primarily linked to future-oriented thinking.

This pattern is consistent with the unselected sample recruited in this study, in which the average willingness to take risks was near the midpoint of the scale (M ≈ 5/10), indicating no bias toward high or low risk-taking.

Importantly, among all questionnaires, willingness to take risks showed the strongest correlation with IU: higher risk-taking willingness was associated with lower IU (see Dekkers et al., 2017, for similar findings).
text.formatted: Importantly, among all questionnaires, willingness to take risks showed the strongest correlation with IU: higher risk-taking willingness was associated with lower IU (see <ref type="bibr">Dekkers et al., 2017, for similar findings)</ref>.

text.text: This aligns with the idea that uncertainty is associated with negative expectancies (Grupe & Nitschke, 2011), whereas willingness to take risks is more closely related to optimism (Dohmen et al., 2023).

text.text: Including positively valenced measures allowed the current study to capture the adaptive, approach-related side of expectancy.
Correlational analyses underscore the value of examining both positive and negative biases separately.

Whereas prior work reported a modest correlation between positive and negative interpretations (Huppert et al., 2003), this correlation was nonsignificant in the present study, suggesting that the two biases may be qualitatively distinct rather than opposite ends of a single continuum.

text.text: A bivalent approach to biased processing may therefore be more ecologically valid and informative (Haj-Ali et al., 2020; Itkes et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A bivalent approach to biased processing may therefore be more ecologically valid and informative <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Haj-Ali et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Itkes et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Correlations with the three DASS factors replicated earlier findings: anxiety, stress, and depression correlated positively with negative interpretations, whereas only depression correlated negatively with positive interpretations.

This pattern aligns with evidence that depression involves both negative interpretations and reduced positive interpretations (Everaert et al., 2017), whereas reduced positive interpretations do not characterize social anxiety (Everaert et al., 2018).

text.text: Together, these findings highlight how different combinations of biased processing may distinguish disorders and may inform more disorder-specific, individually tailored treatments.
The study is grounded in a transdiagnostic and integrative framework, aiming to examine the relationships between three transdiagnostic markers of psychopathology.

Clinically, the results suggest that negative cognitive biases can be considered a transdiagnostic marker of psychopathology, while positive processing can be considered a protective factor (Bean et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Clinically, the results suggest that negative cognitive biases can be considered a transdiagnostic marker of psychopathology, while positive processing can be considered a protective factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bean et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Targeting expectancies during cognitive behavioral therapy or modification could have positive downstream effects, as more negative expectancies were associated with more negative interpretations and more negative symptoms, while more positive expectancies were associated with more positive interpretations and lower psychopathology symptoms.
Ideally, clinical applications would simultaneously target both cognitive biases, as the reduction of one may aid in the reduction of the other, in a selfenforcing cycle.
While CBM for interpretation (CBM-I) has been well-established (Salemink et al., 2023; see also Woud et al., 2012) CBM for expectancies remains an understudied area (e.g., Krans et al., 2019).

text.text: By showing that expectancies are uniquely linked to IU and to symptoms, the present findings provide an empirical rationale for developing and testing expectancy-focused CBM as a complement to CBM-I.
The current study adopted the assumption that, in an unselected sample, participants are likely rate positive outcomes are more expected than negative outcomes.
This is line with previous findings, showing that optimistic expectancies are stronger than pessimistic ones (e.g., Sharot, 2011).
text.formatted: This is line with previous findings, showing that optimistic expectancies are stronger than pessimistic ones (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Sharot, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The current results corroborate this idea, as positive expectancy ratings were significantly higher than negative expectancy ratings.
Yet another argument can be made, according to which pessimism can be used in a defensive manner, to prepare for potential future obstacles (Norem, 2001).
text.formatted: Yet another argument can be made, according to which pessimism can be used in a defensive manner, to prepare for potential future obstacles <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Norem, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: According to this approach, some degree of context-dependent pessimism could in fact be adaptive, as one considers potential negative outcomes and prepares accordingly.
Nonetheless, the overall pattern in this unselected sample indicates a stronger positivity bias in expectancies.

This is in line with a recent study, which found that negative expectancy bias directly predicted anxiety reactivity, and predicted anxiety perseveration indirectly, through the perceived negativity of the event (Tough et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This is in line with a recent study, which found that negative expectancy bias directly predicted anxiety reactivity, and predicted anxiety perseveration indirectly, through the perceived negativity of the event <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Tough et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The authors concluded that negative expectancies should be targeted in intervention, with the aim of improving emotional resilience both in anticipation of and following the anxiety-relevant event.
Examining expectancies in an unselected sample thus establishes a normative baseline of optimistic expectancy.
Negative expectancy bias can then be understood as a clinically relevant deviation from that baseline.
The current study assumed that expectancies temporally precede interpretations, and the task was designed to test this assumption.
However, the correlational design does not allow causal or temporal conclusions.
Future studies could examine the temporal relationship between the two cognitive processes using EEG, which offers high temporal resolution.

Specifically, expectancy-and interpretation-related event-related potentials (ERPs) could clarify whether expectancy-related processing modulates early stages of interpretation (e.g., semantic prediction-error responses to the outcome word; see Abado et al., 2026, for interpretation-relevant ERPs).

text.text: Behaviorally, presenting half of the trials in reverse order (interpretation before expectancy) would test the opposite direction: do biased interpretations of a current event shape expectancies about a similar future event?
This direction is plausible, as training that induces negative interpretations has been found to increase negative expectancies about similar future events (Hirsch et al., 2007).
text.formatted: This direction is plausible, as training that induces negative interpretations has been found to increase negative expectancies about similar future events <ref type="bibr">(Hirsch et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, CBM studies could target interpretations and examine whether modified interpretations lead to modified future-oriented expectancies.

Beyond the relationship between the two biases, the current study focused on one directionality within our theoretical model, in which biased expectancies and interpretations were hypothesized to precede and maintain trait IU.
This reflects our main hypothesis that both cognitive biases, separately and together, contribute to and maintain IU over time.
We assume this relationship is ultimately bidirectional, such that IU, in turn, also helps maintain these biases, but this was not directly tested here.
Future studies could test this using longitudinal designs or experimental manipulations, for instance by manipulating expectancies via feedback and examining downstream effects on IU.
A further limitation concerns the characteristics of the sample.
The sample was relatively homogeneous in terms of ethnicity, nationality, and age range, limiting the generalizability of the findings to more diverse populations.

The study also relied on an unselected community sample, limiting the direct applicability of the findings to clinical populations, in which stronger or qualitatively different associations between expectancy and interpretation biases and trait IU may emerge.

This sampling approach was deliberate and consistent with the study's transdiagnostic approach, as we aimed to examine these associations across the full continuum of IU rather than in a restricted high-IU sample.
Future studies should replicate these findings in more diverse and clinical samples.
To conclude, positively and negatively valenced expectancies predicted subsequent interpretations of the same valence, reflecting a valence-specific carry-over.
Although both biases were associated with trait IU, only expectancies remained associated with IU in the mediation model, and interpretations did not mediate the link between expectancy bias and IU.

Thus, once expectancies are accounted for, interpretations explain no unique variance in IU, which suggests that IU is more closely related to future-oriented thinking than to the interpretation of ambiguity.

The novel paradigm was validated by showing that both biases related to symptom measures in a valence-consistent pattern: positive biases were associated with lower symptoms, and negative biases with higher symptoms.

Together, these findings suggest that expectancies and interpretations are qualitatively distinct processes, each of which can be positively or negatively valenced, and that both may serve as markers of psychopathology when negative and of resilience when positive.

These findings are a step toward understanding how prior expectancies relate to subsequent interpretations, and their bidirectional relationship with one another and with psychopathology warrants further investigation.
